metadata.title: Susquehanna Puts Up $500 Million for ‘Hedging’ World Cup Games

content.text:
(Bloomberg) -- Susquehanna International Group has lined up $500 million to work with institutions that want to use prediction markets to hedge the economic risks associated with various World Cup outcomes.

The Philadelphia-area trading firm said in a statement on Wednesday that it will make the money available to facilitate trades with companies that have a stake in specific teams winning or losing.
Companies that might want to hedge World Cup-related risks include "sponsors, media and broadcast partners, hospitality providers, consumer brands," according to Ric Best, head of prediction markets at Susquehanna.
"Risks could include promotions, rebates, giveaways, or other customer incentives that can be impacted by team performance," Best added.
Prediction markets function much like traditional gambling sites, offering yes-or-no bets on real-world events. But the nascent industry has pushed back against that gambling label, arguing that it provides real social utility by allowing traders to hedge, or buy insurance against things like extreme weather events and election results.
Critics of the industry have seized on the fact that the most popular topics for trading on prediction market exchanges have been sports games, which makes it look a lot more like gambling than economically-motivated trading.
But prediction market exchanges have argued that even trading on sports events can be used by people and companies that have a legitimate economic interest in sports games.
There have been examples of sports-related hedging. Club Atlético Osasuna, a Spanish football team, said last month that it spent €1.2 million ($1.4 million) on a policy that would have paid out €6 million if it was relegated from the top division.
Already, there are signs of broader economic impacts from the winners and losers in the World Cup knockout stages. Beer sales in Latin America could fall short of investor expectations after Brazil and Mexico were both knocked out of the competition, Morgan Stanley analysts said this week.
Susquehanna and its founder, Jeffrey Yass, have been among the most prominent advocates for prediction markets. The firm was the first Wall Street player to announce that it was working as a market maker on Kalshi, now the largest prediction market exchange. Susquehanna has also launched its own prediction market exchange called Rothera, alongside Robinhood Markets Inc.
